question: What is Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) and what does it share between iOS and Android?
answer:
KMP lets you write Kotlin once and compile it for Android, iOS, JVM, JS, Wasm and native desktop; it went Stable in 2023 and is a production choice, not a preview.

It is NOT 'write UI once' — what it shares is everything below the UI:

• Networking — Ktor Client.
• Serialization — kotlinx.serialization.
• Persistence — SQLDelight, Room (KMP support stable since Room 2.7 on Android, iOS, JVM and native), Realm KMP.
• Domain layer and business rules.
• ViewModels — the multiplatform lifecycle artifacts put `ViewModel` in commonMain.
• Coroutines and Flow.

UI stays native (SwiftUI / UIKit on iOS, Compose on Android) — or you share that too with Compose Multiplatform, which is a separate decision.

Gain: one place for business logic, so the two apps cannot quietly disagree about what a rule means. Cost: multi-target Gradle, iOS interop rough edges, and a library ecosystem that is smaller than the JVM one.

question: What are expect/actual declarations in KMP?
answer:
`expect`/`actual` is KMP's mechanism for platform-specific implementations of a shared API.

• In `commonMain` you write `expect class Foo` / `expect fun bar()` — declares the API with no body.
• In each platform source set (`androidMain`, `iosMain`, `jvmMain`) you provide `actual class Foo` / `actual fun bar()` with the platform implementation.
• The compiler ensures all expected declarations have an actual.

Use for things that genuinely need native APIs: file IO, secure storage, DateFormatter, Logger, UUID generation, BluetoothScanner. Don't expect/actual things that have a single common implementation.

Alternative pattern: define an interface in commonMain + provide platform implementations through DI; often cleaner than expect/actual.

question: How does Swift consume KMP code, and where does the Objective-C bridge hurt?
answer:
Kotlin/Native compiles the shared module into an Apple framework that Swift imports like any other module, and almost every pain point comes from the Objective-C bridge in between.

• Suspend functions surface as Swift `async` / `throws` — call them straight from async/await.
• `Flow` surfaces as an opaque Objective-C class, not an `AsyncSequence`. Bridge it with SKIE (Touchlab) or KMP-NativeCoroutines.
• Sealed hierarchies arrive as plain classes, so an exhaustive `switch` degrades into `case let x as ...` casts. SKIE regenerates them as real Swift enums.
• Generics survive but without variance, and Kotlin lambda types show up as awkward closure signatures.
• Package names are flattened into one namespace; resolve collisions with `@ObjCName` and keep internals out of Swift with `@HiddenFromObjC`.
• Value types map roughly: `Long` becomes `KotlinLong`, and `kotlinx-datetime` or decimal types have no natural Swift counterpart.

One thing to stop repeating: the freezing memory model is gone. The current model has been the default since Kotlin 1.7.20 and the legacy one was removed in 1.9.20, so `InvalidMutabilityException` is not a thing you will meet.

Where it is going: direct Swift export skips Objective-C and emits real Swift declarations. It is Alpha — fine for prototypes, not for shipping — and it does not cover coroutines yet, so SKIE or KMP-NativeCoroutines is still the practical answer today.

question: Which libraries would you reach for in a KMP shared module for networking, persistence, DI and logging?
answer:
The KMP ecosystem has converged on one fairly standard stack, and stepping outside it usually costs more than it saves.

• Networking — Ktor Client (Ktor 3.x is the current line) with a per-platform engine: OkHttp on Android, Darwin on iOS, Js on web. JSON through kotlinx.serialization.
• Persistence — SQLDelight 2.x for typed SQL generated from `.sq` files, or Room, whose KMP support went stable in Room 2.7. Key-value: `multiplatform-settings`, or the multiplatform build of DataStore.
• DI — Koin 4.x is the default. Kodein is the alternative, and plain constructor injection is genuinely viable in a shared module.
• Logging — Kermit (Touchlab), which routes to Logcat on Android and os_log on iOS.
• Date and time — `kotlinx-datetime`. Concurrency — `kotlinx-coroutines-core`. Both are official and safe bets.
• Crash and analytics — Sentry KMP, Firebase Crashlytics behind a KMP wrapper, RevenueCat KMP for purchases.
• Swift interop — SKIE and KMP-NativeCoroutines.

Selection rule: check that the library publishes klibs for every target you build, and that its version matches your Kotlin version. Compiler-plugin libraries (Compose, kotlinx-serialization, SQLDelight) break on a Kotlin mismatch far more often than ordinary JVM dependencies do.

question: How high up the stack can KMP sharing reach — can ViewModels and navigation be shared, or do they stay native?
answer:
The ViewModel class is genuinely multiplatform now, and navigation can be shared too — but only if the UI itself is Compose Multiplatform.

ViewModels:
• The multiplatform lifecycle artifacts put `ViewModel` and `viewModelScope` in commonMain. On Android you get the usual configuration-change retention; on iOS nothing retains it for you, so the screen owns the instance and must clear it on disappear.
• Expose `StateFlow<UiState>` plus one `onAction(action)` entry point. That pair is the whole contract native UI binds to, and it keeps platform code dumb.
• Predecessors you will still meet in older codebases: Decompose components, MOKO MVVM, or a hand-rolled class holding its own `CoroutineScope`.

Navigation:
• AndroidX Navigation Compose is published for every Compose Multiplatform target and is stable — same `NavHost`, type-safe routes and deep links as on Android. It needs Compose UI, so it is not an option when iOS is SwiftUI.
• Decompose stays the strongest choice when navigation must live in shared non-Compose code, or when you want component lifecycles and a back stack you can unit-test without a UI.
• Or keep navigation native on both sides and let shared ViewModels drive it. Most KMP-with-native-UI apps do exactly this, because navigation is where platform conventions matter most.

Binding: Compose collects with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`; SwiftUI needs the `StateFlow` bridged to an `AsyncSequence` or an observable wrapper via SKIE or KMP-NativeCoroutines.

question: Your team ships the same product on iOS and Android. How do you decide whether KMP is worth adopting?
answer:
KMP pays off when a large, long-lived business-logic layer would otherwise be written twice, and it costs more than it saves almost everywhere else.

Good fits:
• Business-logic-heavy products on both platforms — banking, e-commerce, ride-hailing, content.
• Long-lived products where the two apps quietly drifting apart is a real and expensive risk.
• Teams comfortable with Gradle and Kotlin, with at least intermediate iOS ability on hand.
• Greenfield, or an existing app you can adopt one module at a time.

Bad fits:
• Short-lived apps. The multi-target build setup dominates a project measured in months.
• UI-dominated apps where shared logic would be a thin slice of the codebase.
• Teams with no iOS expertise — KMP removes none of the work of shipping a polished native iOS app.
• Shops already standardised on Flutter or React Native for cost reasons; KMP shares no UI by default.

Costs to budget: multi-target Gradle and framework packaging, slower iOS builds, the occasional Android-only library with no KMP equivalent, and iOS engineers learning Kotlin plus a second toolchain.

The honest pitch is 'shared business logic, native UI'. If what the business actually wants is 'write the app once', that is Compose Multiplatform or Flutter, not plain KMP.

question: Where does code that iOS and Android share, but the JVM target must not see, actually live in a KMP module?
answer:
In an intermediate source set — the source-set tree is a hierarchy, not a flat list of platforms.

The layers:
• `commonMain` compiles for every target and may only touch the Kotlin stdlib and multiplatform libraries.
• One leaf source set per target: `androidMain`, `iosArm64Main`, `iosSimulatorArm64Main`, `jvmMain`, `wasmJsMain`.
• Intermediate sets sit between them. `iosMain` is the parent of the three iOS targets, `appleMain` covers iOS plus macOS, `nativeMain` covers everything Kotlin/Native compiles. Code there can use Apple platform APIs while still being shared.
• The default hierarchy template creates those intermediate sets for you; older projects wired them by hand with `dependsOn`, and you will still meet that in existing code.
• Every `xxxMain` has a matching `xxxTest`, and `commonTest` runs on all of them.

Dependencies are declared per source set, which is how one API gets three implementations: Ktor core in `commonMain`, the OkHttp engine in `androidMain`, the Darwin engine in `iosMain`.

The rules that trip people up: an `expect` declaration needs an `actual` in every leaf target unless a shared intermediate set covers them all; an Android-only dependency in `commonMain` simply will not compile; and `androidMain` can see the whole JVM and Android SDK, which makes it very easy to accidentally push logic down into it that should have stayed common.

question: What does the iOS app actually depend on — how does the shared Kotlin module get into an Xcode project?
answer:
Kotlin/Native builds the shared module into an Apple framework, and there are three ways to hand that framework to Xcode.

• Direct integration — the default from the project wizard. Xcode gets a run-script build phase calling `./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode`, which builds the architecture the current scheme needs and embeds it. Simplest to set up, and it means every iOS machine needs a JDK and the Gradle build.
• The CocoaPods plugin — the shared module is published as a Pod. Worth it when the iOS app already uses CocoaPods, or when the shared module itself has to depend on a Pod such as a native SDK. Adds Ruby and CocoaPods to the toolchain everyone must install.
• XCFramework plus Swift Package Manager — `assembleSharedXCFramework` produces an `.xcframework` with device and simulator slices, which you publish as a binary target with a checksum. The iOS app then depends on a version number instead of on your Gradle build, which is what you want when the iOS app lives in its own repository or when iOS engineers should never have to touch Kotlin tooling. The price is a publish step in CI and a release process for the shared module.

Two settings that come up in review. `isStatic = true` links the framework into the app binary — faster launch, no dylib to load, but it cannot be shared with app extensions, which need the dynamic form. And `baseName` becomes the Swift module name, so `import Shared` follows from the Gradle file.

Expect the build loop to be the real cost: Kotlin/Native release compilation is slow. Keep day-to-day iOS work on the simulator target and build the full XCFramework only in CI.

question: How do you test a shared KMP module, and why can't you reach for MockK there?
answer:
Tests in `commonTest` compile and run on every target you build, so the same assertions execute on the JVM, on the iOS simulator and on desktop — and that is exactly why JVM-only tooling is off the table.

What works in common test code:
• `kotlin("test")` gives you `@Test` and the `assert*` family on all targets. `./gradlew allTests` runs every target; `jvmTest`, `iosSimulatorArm64Test` and `testDebugUnitTest` run one.
• `runTest` from `kotlinx-coroutines-test` is multiplatform. Inject the dispatcher instead of hard-coding `Dispatchers.IO`, or the test cannot control virtual time.
• Turbine for asserting on `Flow` emissions.
• Ktor's `MockEngine` replaces the HTTP layer without a server, in common code.

What does not: Mockito and MockK are JVM-only, so a `commonTest` cannot mock anything. Write hand-rolled fakes against your own interfaces instead. That constraint is a good argument for defining an interface in `commonMain` and injecting the platform implementation, rather than reaching for `expect`/`actual` everywhere — an interface has a fake, an `actual` does not.

Put genuinely platform-specific tests in `androidTest` or `iosTest`, where the thing under test really is platform code: a Keychain wrapper, a file path, a DataStore.

In CI, a JVM run catches most logic bugs in seconds, but only an iOS simulator run catches Kotlin/Native-specific behaviour, and that needs a macOS runner. Most teams run the JVM target on every PR and the native targets on a slower job.

question: Which coroutine dispatchers exist on iOS in a shared module, and what threading rules still differ from the JVM?
answer:
Kotlin/Native has a normal multithreaded runtime, so `Dispatchers.Main`, `Default` and `IO` all exist on iOS and shared code writes ordinary coroutines.

What maps to what:
• `Dispatchers.Main` dispatches to the main queue, so it is the same guarantee as `DispatchQueue.main`.
• `Dispatchers.Default` is a pool sized by the core count, for CPU work.
• `Dispatchers.IO` exists on Native as well as the JVM, backed by a larger pool for blocking calls.
• `runBlocking` exists on Native, which matters when Swift needs a synchronous call, but it is a deadlock waiting to happen if you use it on the main thread.

What is genuinely different:
• Synchronization primitives: `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock` and `ThreadLocal` are JVM-only. In common code use `Mutex` from coroutines and the multiplatform atomics.
• There is no `Thread` class in common code; `newSingleThreadContext` is the portable way to pin work to one thread.
• Global mutable state is shared across threads exactly as on the JVM, with no compiler help. `@ThreadLocal` on an object makes it per-thread when that is what you want.
• Anything the UI observes must arrive on the main thread. A suspend function exported to Swift resumes on the caller's context, so a background Swift task that then touches UIKit is a crash you own, not a KMP bug.

One thing to stop repeating in interviews: the old freezing memory model, `freeze()` and `InvalidMutabilityException` are gone. The current memory model has been the default for years and the legacy one was removed from the compiler; sharing a mutable object between threads is allowed, and it is your job to synchronize it like anywhere else.

question: The shared module needs Keychain access. How does Kotlin call an Apple API, and when do you need cinterop?
answer:
Kotlin/Native ships generated bindings for the Apple system frameworks, so an iOS source set can import Foundation, UIKit or Security types and call them straight away.

What comes for free:
• `platform.Foundation.NSUserDefaults`, `platform.UIKit.UIDevice`, `platform.Security.SecItemAdd`, `platform.darwin.*` — no configuration, just an import in an iOS source set.
• Objective-C classes become Kotlin classes, categories become extensions, and protocols become interfaces.
• The C-shaped parts need `@OptIn(ExperimentalForeignApi::class)`, and pointers and structs are handled inside `memScoped { }` with `alloc`, `cValue` and `refTo`.

When you need cinterop: a third-party Objective-C or C library that is not a system framework. You write a `.def` file listing its headers and linker options, and the Gradle plugin generates Kotlin bindings from it. If the library is a Pod, the CocoaPods plugin generates that interop for you.

The limitation worth knowing: Kotlin/Native reads Objective-C headers, so a Swift-only API is invisible. Anything declared in Swift without `@objc` exposure cannot be called from Kotlin at all. The way out is to define an interface in `commonMain`, implement it in Swift, and pass the implementation into the shared module — the dependency then points the right way anyway.

Which is the general shape to prefer. Reach for an interface plus dependency injection first; use `expect`/`actual` with platform imports when the implementation is genuinely tiny and has no reason to be swapped.

question: Kotlin/Native is garbage collected and Swift uses ARC. What happens to an object that both sides hold?
answer:
An object crossing the bridge is owned by both runtimes at once, and each of them can only see its own half of the graph.

How it works: a Kotlin object exported to Swift is wrapped in an Objective-C object that ARC retains. While Swift holds it, the Kotlin collector treats it as a root and will not collect it. So the Swift side effectively decides when Kotlin memory is released, and a Swift object captured by Kotlin is kept alive by the Kotlin side symmetrically.

The leak this creates is a cycle across the boundary. A Swift view holds a Kotlin ViewModel; the ViewModel holds a Swift closure — a callback, a Flow collector — that captures `self`. Neither collector can see the whole loop, so nothing is ever freed. Fixes:
• `[weak self]` in any closure you hand to shared code.
• Give every subscription an explicit cancellation handle and call it from `onDisappear` or `deinit`. Long-lived Flow collections started in a shared scope are the usual culprit; SKIE and KMP-NativeCoroutines both return something cancellable for exactly this reason.
• Prefer returning values over registering callbacks, and keep the exported surface small and data-shaped.

On collection behaviour: Kotlin/Native's collector runs concurrently with application threads in current versions, so the long stop-the-world pauses people remember are largely historical. Heavy allocation in a tight loop can still show up as a hitch, and the fix is the same as on any platform — allocate less.

Diagnosing: Xcode Instruments' Allocations and Leaks work, with Kotlin objects appearing under mangled Objective-C names, and Kotlin/Native's own GC logging tells you how often and how long it runs. Decide who owns each lifetime explicitly — usually the screen owns the ViewModel and clears it — rather than hoping two collectors agree.
